claim: Bradykinin (Bk) is a potent inflammatory mediator that causes hyperalgesia.
source: Bradykinin (Bk) is a potent inflammatory mediator that causes hyperalgesia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Dray and Perkins, 1993; Calixto et al., 2000; Manning et al., 1991; Dalmolin et al., 2007).

claim: Bradykinin strongly sensitizes spinal motoneurons.
source: By a combination of patch-clamp recordings and two-photon calcium imaging, we found that Bk strongly sensitizes spinal motoneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Bradykinin-induced sensitization is characterized by an increased ability to generate self-sustained spiking in response to excitatory inputs.
source: Sensitization was characterized by an increased ability to generate self-sustained spiking in response to excitatory inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2F showing self-sustained spiking after Bk application.

claim: Bradykinin sensitizes motoneurons through a dual ionic mechanism including inhibition of a barium-sensitive resting K+ conductance and activation of a nonselective cationic conductance primarily mediated by Na+.
source: Our pharmacological study described a dual ionic mechanism to sensitize motoneurons, including inhibition of a barium-sensitive resting K+ conductance and activation of a nonselective cationic conductance primarily mediated by Na+.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Bradykinin effects involve postsynaptic activation of B2 receptors, G protein activation of phospholipase C, InsP3 synthesis, and calmodulin activation.
source: Examination of the upstream signaling pathways provided evidence for postsynaptic activation of B2 receptors, G protein activation of phospholipase C, InsP3 synthesis, and calmodulin activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Bradykinin excites and/or sensitizes components of the pain pathway, including primary afferent terminals, sensory ganglia, and dorsal horn neurons.
source: It causes hyperalgesia (Manning et al., 1991; Dalmolin et al., 2007) by exciting and/or sensitizing components of the pain pathway, including primary afferent terminals, sensory ganglia, and dorsal horn neurons (Dray and Perkins, 1988; Dray et al., 1988; Thayer et al., 1988; McGuirk and Dolphin, 1992; Rueff and Dray, 1993; Jeftinija, 1994; Cesare et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Systemic blockade of Bk receptors produces analgesia.
source: Consistent with this, systemic blockade of Bk receptors produces analgesia (Steranka et al., 1988; Correa and Calixto, 1993; Perkins et al., 1993; Levy and Zochodne, 2000; Ferreira et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinin, cleaved to Bk by kallikrein in inflammatory responses, is extensively distributed throughout the motor areas of the CNS.
source: However, kinin, cleaved to Bk by kallikrein in inflammatory responses, is extensively distributed throughout the motor areas of the CNS (Walker et al., 1995; Raidoo and Bhoola, 1998) and in particular in the ventral horn of the spinal cord (Lopes and Couture, 1997; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bk receptors have been detected in the membrane of spinal motoneurons.
source: Furthermore, Bk receptors have been detected in the membrane of spinal motoneurons (Lopes et al., 1995) suggesting that pain-related behaviors such as the withdrawal reflex may also arise from a direct Bk-evoked sensitization of motoneurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Direct application of Bk (4–8 µM) above the ventral horn column evoked sustained ventral root activity without inducing antidromic discharge from the dorsal roots.
source: From an in vitro hemicord preparation, the direct application of Bk (4–8 µM) above the ventral horn column (L3–L5, Figure 1A) evoked sustained ventral root activity without inducing antidromic discharge from the dorsal roots (Figure 1B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bk-induced motor output persisted in the presence of the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenate at a concentration that blocked the monosynaptic reflex.
source: This motor output was not exclusively caused by local reverberating circuits, because it persisted in the presence of the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenate at a concentration that blocked the monosynaptic reflex (1.5 mM, Figure 1B, right and Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Subthreshold concentrations of Bk (0.5–1 µM) increased the motoneuron spiking probability in response to supramaximal dorsal root stimulation.
source: With these low concentrations of Bk, the motoneuron spiking probability in response to supramaximal dorsal root stimulation was increased (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 1D-F.

claim: Bk had no effect on the transient short latency reflexes but recruited a long-lasting reflex.
source: Specifically, Bk had no effect on the transient short latency reflexes (number of events: 144 ± 16 for control vs 143 ± 14 during Bk; p = 0.68, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7) but recruited a long-lasting reflex (number of events: 537 ± 104 for control vs 2493 ± 1207 during Bk; p = 0.015, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7) such that the distribution of peristimulus time histograms (PSTHs) shifted from unimodal to bimodal (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: The long-lasting reflex has been previously shown to result from sustained firing of motoneurons involved in muscle spasms.
source: This long-lasting reflex has been previously shown to result from sustained firing of motoneurons involved in muscle spasms (Bennett et al., 2004; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bk increased motoneuron excitability, as reflected by a lower rheobase (528 ± 118 pA for control vs 299 ± 156 pA during Bk; p = 0.028).
source: A few minutes (2–3 min) after the application of Bk, the major effect was an increase in motoneuron excitability, as reflected by a lower rheobase (528 ± 118 pA for control vs 299 ± 156 pA during Bk; p = 0.028, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1 and Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Bk evoked a leftward shift of the f-I curve to lower current values and a slight increase in the slope of the f-I curve (0.05 ± 0.004 Hz/pA for control vs 0.06 ± 0.006 Hz/pA during Bk; p = 0.027).
source: As a consequence, Bk evoked a leftward shift of the f-I curve to lower current values and a slight increase in the slope of the f-I curve (0.05 ± 0.004 Hz/pA for control vs 0.06 ± 0.006 Hz/pA during Bk; p = 0.027, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2B.

claim: The higher motoneuron excitability was associated with an apparent increase in input resistance (55.6 ± 5.4 MΩ for control vs 62.9 ± 7.2 MΩ during Bk; p = 0.004).
source: The higher motoneuron excitability was associated with an apparent increase in input resistance (55.6 ± 5.4 MΩ for control vs 62.9 ± 7.2 MΩ during Bk; p = 0.004, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1) as seen by the increased slope of the voltage responses to hyperpolarizing pulses (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Bk lowered the threshold for action potential generation (−50.0 ± 2.1 mV for the control vs −52.8 ± 2.5 mV during Bk; p = 0.009).
source: Bk lowered the threshold for action potential generation (−50.0 ± 2.1 mV for the control vs −52.8 ± 2.5 mV during Bk; p = 0.009, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1) which, although not wider (0.51 ± 0.02 ms for control vs 0.51 ± 0.02 ms during Bk; p = 0.77, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1), was smaller in amplitude (67.0 ± 2.3 mV for control vs 63.6 ± 2.2 mV during Bk; p = 0.049, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1 and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2D.

claim: The amplitude of the sag was not affected by Bk (12 ± 2.6% for control vs 12.3 ± 2.5% during Bk; p = 0.95).
source: Hyperpolarizing current steps evoked a marked depolarizing sag (inward rectification) which is often associated with activation of the hyperpolarization-activated inward current Ih (Figure 2A); the amplitude of the sag was not affected by Bk (12 ± 2.6% for control vs 12.3 ± 2.5% during Bk; p = 0.95, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2A.

claim: The medium afterhyperpolarization (mAHP) was enhanced both in amplitude and duration by Bk.
source: However, the medium afterhyperpolarization (mAHP) was enhanced both in amplitude and duration (amplitude: −9.1 ± 0.9 mV for the control vs −11.2 ± 1.5 mV for Bk, p = 0.02; duration: 41.1 ± 2.5 ms for control vs 48.6 ± 3.4 ms for Bk, p = 0.014; Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2E.

claim: Bk increased the amplitude of the post-stimulus sADP (11.2 ± 1.4 mV for control vs 18 ± 2.6 mV for Bk; p = 0.008).
source: Bk increased the amplitude of the post-stimulus sADP (11.2 ± 1.4 mV for control vs 18 ± 2.6 mV for Bk; p = 0.008, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1) and triggered self-sustained spiking in all motoneurons tested (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2F.

claim: Bk triggered self-sustained spiking in all motoneurons tested.
source: Bk increased the amplitude of the post-stimulus sADP (11.2 ± 1.4 mV for control vs 18 ± 2.6 mV for Bk; p = 0.008, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 10 cells; Table 1) and triggered self-sustained spiking in all motoneurons tested (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Among 200 lumbar motoneurons recorded, 154 (77%) displayed a reversible membrane depolarization in response to Bk.
source: To test whether Bk directly excites motoneurons, we recorded activity from 200 lumbar motoneurons in response to a brief (≤2 min) bath application of Bk (8 µM). Among them, 154 (77%) displayed a reversible membrane depolarization (Figure 3A) while the remaining 46 had no responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The amplitude of the Bk-induced depolarization was not changed after blockade of glutamatergic input with kynurenate (1.5 mM) or by CNQX (10 µM) and AP-5 (20 µM).
source: The amplitude of the depolarization was not changed after blockade of glutamatergic input with kynurenate (1.5 mM) or by CNQX (10 µM) and AP-5 (20 µM) (92.9 ± 17.8% of the control; p = 0.62, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 4 cells; Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Bk-induced depolarization persisted in the presence of 0.5–1 μM TTX.
source: Supporting this idea, the Bk-induced depolarization persisted in the presence of 0.5–1 μM TTX (12.9 ± 0.6 mV; n = 154; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effects of Bk were fully reversible without tachyphylaxis.
source: The effects of Bk were fully reversible without tachyphylaxis; when Bk was repetitively applied at intervals of 20 min, the amplitude of the second response was not significantly reduced from the first response (95.6 ± 13.9% of the first response; p = 0.22, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7 cells; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spantide did not attenuate Bk-induced responses (response in spantide 92.1 ± 18% of control response; p = 0.62).
source: Spantide did not attenuate Bk-induced responses (response in spantide 92.1 ± 18% of control response; p = 0.62, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 4 cells; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The selective B1 agonist, Lys-[Des-Arg9]-Bk, at concentrations as high as 3 µM, failed to induce a significant depolarization (2.2 ± 0.6 mV, n = 10 cells).
source: Under TTX, the selective B1 agonist, Lys-[Des-Arg9]-Bk (Ki = 1.7 nM; Marceau et al., 1998), at concentrations as high as 3 µM, failed to induce a significant depolarization (2.2 ± 0.6 mV, n = 10 cells; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The selective B2 receptor agonist [Hyp]3-Bk, used at 2 µM evoked a membrane depolarization similar to responses evoked by Bk (11.2 ± 1.5 mV n = 10 cells for [Hyp]3-Bk vs 12.9 ± 0.6 mV, n = 154 for Bk; p = 0.48).
source: In contrast, the selective B2 receptor agonist [Hyp]3-Bk (Ki = 314 pM; Windischhofer and Leis, 1997), used at 2 µM evoked a membrane depolarization similar to responses evoked by Bk (11.2 ± 1.5 mV n = 10 cells for [Hyp]3-Bk vs 12.9 ± 0.6 mV, n = 154 for Bk; p = 0.48, Mann–Whitney test; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The response to Bk was almost abolished by 2 µM HOE 140 (11.7 ± 2.7% of the control depolarization; p = 0.03).
source: Consistent with an involvement of B2 receptors, the response to Bk was almost abolished by 2 µM HOE 140 (11.7 ± 2.7% of the control depolarization; p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 3D), a potent and selective B2 receptor antagonist (IC50 = 420 pM; Eggerickx et al., 1992).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Bk reversibly generated an inward current whose time course was similar to that seen in current-clamp recordings.
source: Under these conditions, Bk reversibly generated an inward current whose time course was similar to that seen in current-clamp recordings (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The inward current amplitude was steeply dependent on Bk concentration, with an EC50 of 680 nM and maximal amplitude (322 ± 26 pA, n = 14) at 4–8 μM.
source: The inward current amplitude was steeply dependent on Bk concentration, with an EC50 of 680 nM and maximal amplitude (322 ± 26 pA, n = 14) at 4–8 μM (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A significant Bk-induced decrease in the slope conductance was observed in I/V curves (18.7 ± 2.4 pA/mV before Bk vs 15.6 ± 2.2 pA/mV during Bk; p = 0.016).
source: A significant Bk-induced decrease in the slope conductance was observed in I/V curves (18.7 ± 2.4 pA/mV before Bk vs 15.6 ± 2.2 pA/mV during Bk; p = 0.016, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7 cells; Figure 4C), an effect often interpreted as a consequence of the inhibition of a K+ conductance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The linear I/V relationship of the Bk-sensitive-current reversed at an extrapolated value close to the predicted equilibrium potential for K+ (Ek: −100 mV).
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the linear I/V relationship of the Bk-sensitive-current (obtained by subtracting the control from the Bk currents: Figure 4C, orange line with open circles) reversed at an extrapolated value close to the predicted equilibrium potential for K+ (Ek: −100 mV).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The combination of traditional voltage-gated K+ channel blockers and the Ca2+-activated K+ channel blocker apamin did not change either the Bk-induced decrease in slope conductance or the peak depolarization magnitude.
source: The combination of traditional voltage-gated K+ channel blockers [TEA (10 mM), 4-aminopyridine (2 mM), the HCN-channel blocker ZD7288 (20 µM)] and the Ca2+-activated K+ channel blocker apamin (100 nM), did not change either the Bk-induced decrease in slope conductance (33.2 ± 3.2 pA/mV before Bk vs 21.1 ± 2.3 pA/mV during Bk; p = 0.02, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 15 cells; Figure 4D1) or the peak depolarization magnitude measured in current clamp from −70 mV (94.5 ± 15.8% of the control; p = 0.54, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7 cells; Figure 4D2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 4D1 and 4D2.

claim: Under high [K+]o, Bk still induced a depolarization from −70 mV without a measurable change in input resistance, but the depolarization was significantly smaller than that seen in normal aCSF (64.2 ± 17.7% of the control value; p = 0.047).
source: Under high [K+]o, Bk still induced a depolarization from −70 mV without a measurable change in input resistance (45.3 ± 13.9 MΩ before Bk vs 46.5 ± 13.2 MΩ during Bk; p = 0.81, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7 cells). However, the depolarization was significantly smaller than that seen in normal aCSF (64.2 ± 17.7% of the control value measured in normal aCSF; p = 0.047, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7 cells; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The residual Bk-induced depolarization observed in high [K+]o disappeared after reducing [Na+]o from 152 to 26 mM with equimolar choline-chloride (4.1 ± 2.8% of the control value; p = 0.016).
source: The residual Bk-induced depolarization observed in high [K+]o appears to be sodium-mediated because it disappeared after reducing [Na+]o from 152 to 26 mM with equimolar choline-chloride (4.1 ± 2.8% of the control value measured in high [K+]o; p = 0.016, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 7 cells; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Quinidine induced a large depolarization (+6.8 ± 3.9 mV, n = 6 cells) and reduced the slope conductance itself (22 ± 3.8 pA/mV before quinidine vs 14.2 ± 3.4 pA/mV during quinidine; p < 0.01).
source: Quinidine induced alone a large depolarization (+6.8 ± 3.9 mV, n = 6 cells, not shown) and reduced the slope conductance itself (22 ± 3.8 pA/mV before quinidine vs 14.2 ± 3.4 pA/mV during quinidine; p < 0.01, One-way ANOVA test, n = 6 cells; Figure 5A1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A1.

claim: Quinidine prevented the slope conductance decrease induced by Bk and partially occluded the Bk-induced membrane depolarization (57.7 ± 21.5% of control; p = 0.03).
source: Further, quinidine prevented the slope conductance decrease induced by Bk (14.2 ± 3.4 pA/mV for control vs 13 ± 3 pA/mV during Bk; p > 0.05, One-way ANOVA test, n = 6; Figure 5A1) and partially occluded the Bk-induced membrane depolarization (57.7 ± 21.5% of control; p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6; Figure 5A2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 5A1 and 5A2.

claim: Acidification to pH 6.4 did not significantly decrease the slope conductance itself and the response to Bk was not affected by acidification.
source: As expected, acidification induced a membrane depolarization (+4.3 ± 0.6 mV, n = 5 cells, not shown) but did not significantly decrease the slope conductance itself (26.4 ± 6.9 pA/mV at pH 7.4 vs 21.2 ± 5.2 pA/mV at pH 6.4; p > 0.05, One-Way ANOVA test, n = 5 cells; Figure 5B1). Furthermore, the response to Bk was not affected by acidification to pH 6.4, that is, the slope conductance decrease (21.2 ± 5.2 pA/mV for control vs 11.2 ± 3.6 pA/mV during Bk; p < 0.05, One-Way ANOVA test, n = 5 cells; Figure 5B1) and the membrane depolarization from −70 mV were not affected (92.6 ± 16.0% of values at pH 7.4; p = 0.69, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 5B2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 5B1 and 5B2.

claim: Bath application of Ba2+ (300 µM) caused a significant depolarization (+6.6 ± 0.8 mV, n = 6 cells) and decreased the slope conductance (29.3 ± 3.2 pA/mV for control vs 22 ± 2.6 pA/mV during barium; p < 0.01).
source: The Bath application of Ba2+ (300 µM) caused a significant depolarization (+6.6 ± 0.8 mV, n = 6 cells, not shown) and also by itself decreased the slope conductance (29.3 ± 3.2 pA/mV for control vs 22 ± 2.6 pA/mV during barium; p < 0.01, One-Way ANOVA test, n = 6 cells; Figure 5C1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C1.

claim: Ba2+ reduced but did not prevent the slope conductance decrease induced by Bk and it occluded the Bk-induced membrane depolarization from −70 mV (58.6 ± 17.7% of control; p = 0.03).
source: Ba2+ reduced but did not prevent the slope conductance decrease induced by Bk (22 ± 2.6 pA/mV for control vs 18.1 ± 2.4 pA/mV during Bk; p < 0.05, One-Way ANOVA test, n = 6; Figure 5C1), and it occluded the Bk-induced membrane depolarization from −70 mV (58.6 ± 17.7% of control; p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 5C2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 5C1 and 5C2.

claim: In high [K+]o, the Bk-induced depolarization from −70 mV was nearly abolished by 10 µM ruthenium red (16.6 ± 6.5% of control response; p = 0.03).
source: In high [K+]o, the Bk-induced depolarization from −70 mV (where the effect of the resting K+ current is minimized) was nearly abolished by 10 µM ruthenium red (16.6 ± 6.5% of control response; p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Lowering the temperature from 34 to 24°C induced a significant decrease in the Bk-induced depolarization at −70 mV in high [K+]o (26.2 ± 9.8% of control values; p = 0.03).
source: This apparent ICaN was also thermosensitive because lowering the temperature from 34 to 24°C induced a significant decrease in the Bk-induced depolarization at −70 mV in high [K+]o (26.2 ± 9.8% of control values; p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Bk induced a rise in [Ca2+]i (13.4 ± 0.7% ΔF/F) in 65% of motoneuron somata (n = 177 out of 272 cells; n = 5 slices).
source: Bk induced a rise in [Ca2+]i (13.4 ± 0.7% ΔF/F) in 65% of motoneuron somata (n = 177 out of 272 cells; n = 5 slices), with very slow decay times (Figure 6B,C); there was no change in [Ca2+]i in the remaining motoneurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: After Bk application, the proximal dendrites up to 50 µm away from the soma showed a clear rise in [Ca2+]i (49.8 ± 8.7% ΔF/F; n = 5 cells), which was followed with a delay by the somatic response (44.5e ± 8.9% ΔF/F; n = 5 cells).
source: After Bk application, the proximal dendrites up to 50 µm away from the soma showed a clear rise in [Ca2+]i (49.8 ± 8.7% ΔF/F; n = 5 cells; Figure 6E,F; red trace), which was followed with a delay by the somatic response (44.5e ± 8.9% ΔF/F; n = 5 cells; Figure 6E,F; blue trace).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: A single action potential induced a [Ca2+]i rise significantly higher in the proximal dendrites than in the soma (Casoma = 6.1 ± 1.5% ΔF/F; Cadendrite = 16.9 ± 3.6% ΔF/F; n = 5 cells; p = 0.02).
source: Our results show that a single action potential induced a [Ca2+]i rise significantly higher in the proximal dendrites than in the soma (Casoma = 6.1 ± 1.5% ΔF/F; Cadendrite = 16.9 ± 3.6% ΔF/F; n = 5 cells; p = 0.02, Student's paired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The Bk-induced rise in [Ca2+]i was significantly higher than that evoked by a single action potential in both the soma and the dendrites (p = 0.003 and p = 0.008).
source: The Bk-induced rise in [Ca2+]i was significantly higher than that evoked by a single action potential in both the soma and the dendrites (p = 0.003 and p = 0.008, Student's unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Cadmium blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels did not prevent the depolarization induced by Bk (83 ± 9.7%, of control depolarization; p = 0.46).
source: Similarly, the effects of Bk on motoneurons were not significantly reduced by cadmium blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels (100 µM; 83 ± 9.7%, of control depolarization; p = 0.46, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 8 cells; Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: After intracellular perfusion of BAPTA (10 mM), the depolarization induced by Bk declined to 28.8 ± 6.4% of its original value 20 minutes after establishing the whole cell recording (p = 0.008).
source: 20 minutes after establishing the whole cell recording, the depolarization induced by Bk declined to 28.8 ± 6.4% of its original value (p = 0.008, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 8 cells; Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: After diffusion of GDPβS into the cell, the subsequent application of Bk failed to induce a depolarization (9.7 ± 5.7% of control, p = 0.03).
source: After diffusion of GDPβS into the cell, the subsequent application of Bk failed to induce a depolarization (9.7 ± 5.7% of control, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: After 7 hr of preincubation with either the Gi inhibitor pertussis toxin (PTX, 2 µg.ml−1) or the Gs inhibitor cholera toxin (CTX, 2 µg.ml−1) the magnitude of Bk responses was not disturbed.
source: We showed that Bk signaling is independent of Gi or Gs protein by showing that after 7 hr of preincubation with either the Gi inhibitor pertussis toxin (PTX, 2 µg.ml−1) or the Gs inhibitor cholera toxin (CTX, 2 µg.ml−1) the magnitude of Bk responses was not disturbed (CTX: 14.7 ± 2.7 mV, n = 5 cells, p = 0.6; PTX: 16.7 ± 1.8 mV, n = 4 cells p = 0.3; control: 12.9 ± 0.6 mV, n = 54 cells, Mann–Whitney test; data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: U73122 (10 µM) greatly reduced Bk-induced depolarization (24.6 ± 4% of control; p = 0.03).
source: U73122 (10 µM) greatly reduced Bk-induced depolarization (24.6 ± 4% of control; p = 0.03, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Intrapipette loading with xestospongin (2.5 mM) induced a significant reduction of the Bk-induced depolarization (38.8 ± 17.4% of control, p = 0.015).
source: Intrapipette loading with xestospongin (2.5 mM) induced a significant reduction of the Bk-induced depolarization (38.8 ± 17.4% of control, p = 0.015, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 8 cells, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Bath application of chelerythrine (10 µM) or intracellular diffusion of PKC 19–36 (10 µM) did not reduce the Bk response (pooled data:10.5 ± 17.8% of control, p = 1).
source: In contrast, bath application of chelerythrine (10 µM) or intracellular diffusion of PKC 19–36 (10 µM), two potent inhibitors of PKC (IC50 = 0.66 µM and 0.3 µM respectively; Herbert et al., 1990; Smith et al., 1990), did not reduce the Bk response (pooled data:10.5 ± 17.8% of control, p = 1, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 5 cells 3 with chelerythrine and 2 with PKC 19–36, Figure 7D) indicating that the DAG pathway is not involved.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Either 10 µM bath application of H89 or 10 µM intracellular administration of PKA 6–22 did not reduce the Bk response (95.9 ± 12.9% of control, p = 0.31).
source: Similar results were collected with either 10 µM bath application of H89 or 10 µM intracellular administration of PKA 6–22 (95.9 ± 12.9% of control, p = 0.31, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells 3 with H89 and 3 with PKA 6–22, Figure 7E), two potent blockers of PKA (IC50 = 0.14 µM and 2 nM respectively; (Glass et al., 1989; Davies et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Application of W-7 (100 µM), a membrane permeable CaM inhibitor, abolished the Bk-induced depolarization (3.1 ± 5%; p = 0.02).
source: Supporting a role for CaM in the Bk response, application of W-7 (100 µM), a membrane permeable CaM inhibitor (IC50 ≈ 30 µM; Hidaka et al., 1981), abolished the Bk-induced depolarization (3.1 ± 5%; p = 0.02, Wilcoxon paired test, n = 6 cells; Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The Bk-evoked motoneuron depolarization was not significantly affected by KN-93 (10 μM), a potent CaMKII inhibitor (KN-93: 10.9 ± 2.4 mV, n = 6 cells; Control: 12.9 ± 0.6 mV, n = 154; p = 0.52).
source: However, the Bk-evoked motoneuron depolarization was not significantly affected by KN-93 (KN-93: 10.9 ± 2.4 mV, n = 6 cells; Control: 12.9 ± 0.6 mV, n = 154; p = 0.52, Mann–Whitney test, data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Bk has long been shown to depolarize sensory neurons by inhibiting K+ channels.
source: Bk has long been shown to depolarize sensory neurons by inhibiting K+ channels (Weinreich, 1986; Brown and Higashida, 1988; Jones et al., 1995; Villarroel, 1996; Cruzblanca et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The most likely candidates for the Ba2+-sensitive K+ current are TWIK and THIK channels.
source: Thus the most likely candidates for the Ba2+-sensitive K+ current are TWIK and THIK channels (Chavez et al., 1999; Patel et al., 2000; Rajan et al., 2001; Lloyd et al., 2009) though TWIK channels are much more sensitive to Ba2+ (IC50: 0.1 mM) than THIK (IC50: ∼1 mM) (Patel and Honore, 2001; Rajan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bk has been shown to activate different classes of TRP channels.
source: Consistent with this, Bk has been shown to activate different classes of TRP channels (Premkumar and Ahern, 2000; Delmas et al., 2002; Sugiura et al., 2002; Bandell et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2008) and to induce a Na+-mediated ICaN in cultured spinal sensory neurons (Burgess et al., 1989; Dray et al., 1992; McGehee et al., 1992; Seabrook et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several groups have provided data in different systems suggesting that Bk depolarizes neurons by triggering a PLC signaling pathway giving rise to the InsP3-dependent release of Ca2+ and DAG.
source: Several groups have provided data in different systems suggesting that Bk depolarizes neurons by triggering a PLC signaling pathway giving rise to the InsP3-dependent release of Ca2+ and DAG (Yano et al., 1984, 1985; Derian and Moskowitz, 1986; Francel and Dawson, 1986; Francel et al., 1987; Jackson et al., 1987; Thayer et al., 1988; Perney and Miller, 1989; Gutowski et al., 1991; Hall, 1992; Premkumar and Ahern, 2000; Ferreira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Following traumatic injury, increases in the concentration of kinins in the spinal cord might predispose motoneurons to express self-sustained plateau potentials, thereby contributing to muscle spasms.
source: Following traumatic injury, increases in the concentration of kinins in the spinal cord (Xu et al., 1991) might thus predispose motoneurons to express self-sustained plateau potentials, thereby contributing to muscle spasms (Nickolls et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: Chronic spinal rats show the emergence of long-lasting reflexes in vivo.
source: In keeping with this hypothesis, chronic spinal rats show the emergence of long-lasting reflexes in vivo (Murray et al., 2010), similar to those we recorded in response to Bk in vitro (see Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and comparison to experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: The spinal cord represents a relevant site of action for kinins to produce hypernociception.
source: The spinal cord also represents a relevant site of action for kinins to produce hypernociception (Steranka et al., 1988; Perkins et al., 1993; Ferreira et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The flexor withdrawal motor reflex has commonly been used as a surrogate pain model.
source: The flexor withdrawal motor reflex has commonly been used as a surrogate pain model (Barrot, 2012); however, the contribution of motoneuron hyperexcitability has never been questioned.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The neonatal response to nociception differs from that found in adults.
source: It is also important to emphasize that the neonatal response to nociception differs from that found in adults (Fitzgerald, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Experiments were performed on neonatal (0–7 days old) Wistar rats of either sex.
source: Experiments were performed on neonatal (0–7 days old) Wistar rats of either sex.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental subjects.

claim: The peak current density was 1.5 ± 0.15 pA/pF (n = 14).
source: The peak current density was 1.5 ± 0.15 pA/pF (n = 14).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Neonatal rat lumbar motoneurons show marked bistability at temperatures above 30°C, characterized by their ability to generate a slow afterdepolarization (sADP) that outlasted a brief high amplitude depolarizing pulse.
source: In a recent publication, we demonstrated that at temperatures above 30°C, neonatal rat lumbar motoneurons show marked bistability, characterized by their ability to generate a slow afterdepolarization (sADP) that outlasted a brief high amplitude depolarizing pulse (Bouhadfane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The Bk-induced increase in [Ca2+]i was likely caused by Ca2+ released from intracellular stores rather than by Ca2+ influx through Ca2+-permeable membrane channels.
source: Combined with our calcium imaging results, these experiments suggest that the Bk-induced increase in [Ca2+]i observed in our experiments was likely caused by Ca2+ released from intracellular stores rather than by Ca2+ influx through Ca2+-permeable membrane channels.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing that cadmium blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels did not prevent Bk effects, while BAPTA reduced them.

claim: The initial rise of [Ca2+]i at the dendritic level is consistent with the location of B2 receptors in the peripheral processes of motoneurons.
source: The initial rise of [Ca2+]i at the dendritic level supports this hypothesis and is consistent with the location of B2 receptors in the peripheral processes of motoneurons (Lopes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Microglial cells express functional Bk receptors and Bk can act as a neuron-glia signaling molecule.
source: On the other hand, microglial cells express functional Bk receptors (Noda et al., 2003; Ifuku et al., 2007) and Bk can act as a neuron-glia signaling molecule (Parpura et al., 1994; Heblich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bath-applied Bk may activate glial cells resulting in the release of an unidentified chemical substance which may mediate some of Bk's effects on motoneurons.
source: Therefore, we cannot be rule out the possibility that bath-applied Bk activates glial cells resulting in the release of an unidentified chemical substance which may mediate some of Bk's effects on motoneurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging a limitation of the study.
